## Problem 1: Classification Trees

In this problem, we will create a classification tree to predict a diagnosis for breast cancer as either malignant (i.e., harmful, cancerous) or benign (i.e., not cancerous). To build such a model, we will use data from a 1993 study of image data on breast tumors in which "features" (i.e., predictors) were extracted from the images, as well as a diagnosis made by a medical professional. You can load the training data by running the following code chunk. 

```{r}
wdbc <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pearce790/Math141/refs/heads/main/wdbc.csv")[,-1]
wdbc_test <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pearce790/Math141/refs/heads/main/wdbc_test.csv")[,-1]
```

There are 419 observations. For each, we have a `Diagnosis` and 30 other unnamed predictors variables. The data source and original study can be found [here](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/17/breast+cancer+wisconsin+diagnostic) and [here](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Nuclear-feature-extraction-for-breast-tumor-Street-Wolberg/53f0fbb425bc14468eb3bf96b2e1d41ba8087f36). *As a final disclaimer, I do not condone the blind use of statistical models to make medical decisions! Such models may be useful but should, in nearly all contexts, aide the decision-making of a medical professional and not replace their expertise entirely.*


a.  Fit a *deep* tree to the training data (`deep_tree`) and *plot* the tree.

b.  Prune `deep_tree` (`pruned_tree`) appropriately. Justify the way you pruned your tree using an appropriate plot.

c.  Misdiagnosing a malignant tumor as benign has potentially devastating implications (i.e., falsely telling someone they're healthy when, in fact, they require medical attention for a life-threatening condition). Fit a tree model to your training data that penalizes mistakes of this kind 10 times more than the other type of misdiagnosis (`loss_tree`)

d.  We now have three tree models: `deep_tree`, `pruned_tree`, and `loss_tree`. For each, create a confusion matrix and calculate the incorrect classification error rate *based on the test data* (`wdbc_test`) to assess the accuracy of each model when applied to new patients.

e.  Comment on your results from part d. Which model has the lowest test error? Are the rates of "devastatingly bad" misdiagnoses substantially different between the models? Which model would you prefer?




## Problem 2: Comparing Regression Models with `College` Data

For this exercise, we will use the `College` data from the ISLR package. Familiarize yourself with this dataset before performing analysis. We will attempt to predict the `Outstate` variable, which indicates the college's out-of-state tuition rate in 1995. Load the data with the following code, which also creates a 70-30% training-test split.

```{r}
data("College")
set.seed(1)
which_train <- sample(1:nrow(College),0.7*nrow(College))
college_train <- College[which_train,]
college_test <- College[-which_train,]
```

a.  Create the following **five** models on the training data and tune the relevant tuning parameters (e.g., $\alpha$ in tree-based methods) using cross-validation.

  - A well-tuned LASSO model
  - A pruned regression tree (no bagging, boosting, or random forests)
  - A `randomForest()` model that performs only bagging and no actual random forests (recall that bagging is the special case of random forests with $m = p$). 
  - A `randomForest()` model that uses $m = p/3$.
  - A well-tuned boosted tree model.

b.  Calculate the test RMSE for each model and compare. Which model performs best on test data? 

c.  For the first two models, which features were utilized?

d.  For the ensemble models, display variable importance plots. Which variable is *most* important in each model?

e.  Summarize what you learned while completing this problem *using non-technical language* that could be understood by someone working in the Admissions office at Reed College.
